items.title: 68163_Tom Whaley oral history interview
items.q: when Enrico Caruso would come to Boston at the opera house, he'd come down there and Sunday afternoon at 2 o'clock and he'd stand up there and direct -- we'd play all the overtures... he'd give us $200 and divide it amongst the band.

ctx.x: So that's where you learned how to be so tough on us youngsters when we'd come along.

Oh, yeah, when I came to New York I used to tell everybody learn how to read. If you can't read, you can't read because up until the war in 1918 the white musicians weren't known in Boston, everything was colored. Colored musicians had all the jobs and then after the world war there was a -- the white musicians swept us away, but in 1912 I got a job out in Reading, Massachusetts, out at a road house and every Sunday when Enrico Caruso would come to Boston at the opera house, he'd come down there and Sunday…
And then we'd drink champagne and then when he'd get ready to go he'd give us $200 and divide it amongst the band. And 13, 14, Leroy Johnson was playing down to roadhouse
